item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm going to be a little harsh. But before I start, I want to make it clear that this is only because I like the piece: it's got a great central concept, a strong open with clean technical polish, and action that moves at a brisk pace. The story is fun, the dialogue is quick, and it doesn't waste any of my time. All A++.

However, the prose after your opening is a bit of a slog. On top of some grammatical and punctuation errors, you've got a lot of clauses (sometimes clauses in clauses) that are slowing things down. You use dialogue tags in places where they weaken the prose, and there's an over-reliance on compound sentences and -ing words (which, again, weaken the prose). I'm going to give you some examples, and briefly sweep through some of the piece's more obvious errors.

Again: I'm going to be a bit harsh, but keep in mind that's because I like this piece and want to see it succeed. Good, clean, solid prose is hard — and a rarity here. I'm only picking on your piece because it managed to catch my attention and hold it despite these issues. I wouldn't bother with this if I didn't think it wasn't good!

Okay, so I'll dig right in:

+ show block
– hide block

The cabin, constructed in a futurist organic style, spiraled out so that a portion of of each floor hung over open water. On the third story, which was entirely given over to a spacious covered deck, Sarah Hughes, Mobile Task Force Tau-5 ("Samsara") commander, sipped her coffee and looked out through the wire screen onto the pond. Chen was in a canoe instructing Onru and Munru on how to fish, all three of them laughing in the sun. All the way from the kitchen, on the ground floor, she could smell some delicious Kurdish dish that Ghazi was teaching to Irantu. Face screwed up in unself-conscious concentration, Nanku was sitting on a couch a couple of meters away, trying to paint a duck in watercolor. Hughes wondered, not for the first time, if this was really any different from having a family.

Let's start by exposing the skeletal structure of this opening paragraph. I'm going to swap out the important bits of your prose with letters so you can see what its bare bones look like:

The A, constructed in B, spiraled out so that C was over D. On E, which was F, G, H's commander, sipped I and looked out through J at K. L was instructing M and N on O, all three of them P in the Q. All the way from R, on the S, G could T some U that V was teaching to W. X screwed up in Y, Z was A, trying to B. G wondered, not for the first time, if this was really any different from C.

Just read this aloud and you should start to see a problem. "This, which is that, did that. On this, which was that, they, the commander of this, did that to that." If you want the prose to flow, you need to break up your clauses. You need some simple sentences. At the very least, you need to untangle that second sentence — those nested clauses are straight up brutal.

Let me rewrite this and untangle some of your clauses. You don't have to do it this way, obviously, but I want to give you a sense of how I think your opening could work a bit more cleanly:

The cabin was constructed in a futurist organic style. It spiraled out so that a portion of each floor hung over open water. On the third story, Sarah Hughes, Mobile Task Force Tau-5's commander, sipped her coffee and looked down through the wire screen onto the pond. Chen was in a canoe instructing Onru and Munru how to fish; all three laughed in the sun. From the first floor kitchen, Hughes could smell some delicious Kurdish dish that Ghazi was teaching to Irantu. Nanku sat a couple of meters behind Hughes — face screwed up in unself-conscious concentration, trying to paint a duck in watercolor. Not for the first time, Hughes wondered if this was really any different from having a family.

Now, I think that this opening could still be better, but I didn't want to change the fundamental prose — just untangle the clauses and show how the result reads much more cleanly.

Moving on:

"Explain," ordered Hughes as they took the stairs to the second floor.

You need a comma here.

The stairs let out out into a landing with a large bay window overlooking the water, framed by white walls made from an ultra-toughened metal alloy.

I took the second out 'out', but also I adjusted the ending phrase — because 'ultra-toughened white metal alloy walls' is a mouthful.

He switched on his bunk lamp and swung his legs onto the floor as she closed the door.

This is 'swung', not 'swinging'.

It was a black Ford Explorer, with tinted windows. It looked like a rental.

This was a run-on, so I broke it apart.

"Ma'am, this is a restricted area, I am going to have to ask you to return to the guardhouse the way you came." Quinn said.

I'm going to be a jerk and push my own essay for writing tales — specifically, the bit where I talk about dialogue tags. Always get rid of dialogue tags when you don't need them. And you don't need them here: It is very clear who's speaking (these are not words a woman driving up to a guard-post would be saying to a male guard; these are words a male guard would be saying to the woman who just drove up).

"Now honey, we don't need to do that, we are exactly where we are supposed to be be." she answered.

Even if you want to keep the dialogue tag from before, you don't need this one. It's clear who he's talking to, and it's clear who would reply (the woman).

"Appointed," said the others in unison.

This one you need. Just pointing it out as an example of a case when you do need a tag (and you used one!).

"Ma'am, we can… sense… an entity is now present,", answered by Irantu as he cocked his head to the side, listening for something.

Comma goes inside the quotes. I've seen cases where people do it differently, but you've been putting the commas inside the quotes up till now — so you need to be consistent.

Shaking her head, Nanku said, "Two entities."

I want to show you an example of what I mean about how dialogue tags and -ing words can weaken prose. Here's what you wrote. Now, let's take out the dialogue tag and the -ing word ("Shaking"). Here's what we get instead:

Nanku shook her head. "Two entities."

The difference is like night-and-day. The original has three beats — three pauses — and one of those pauses is only there to tell us who's speaking. The new version has two pauses, and doesn't need to tell us who's speaking (we can instantly tell from the use of Nanku's name in the sentence prior). It's quicker, shorter, and much stronger.

"No ma'am, I don't think so," he said as Nanku shook her head again, "They seem to be… trapped?"

This is confusing. I think… Irantu is the 'he', here? I'm 75% sure. But you should make it explicit:

"No, ma'am. I don't think so." Irantu paused to think. Behind him, Nanku shook her head again. "They seem to be… trapped?"

The next part — the part that's just effectively a dialogue script — is strong, polished, and clean. Any changes I'd suggest would be trifling. I'm pointing this out to emphasize how your technical writing and dialogue aren't the issue here — those aspects are strong, and what makes the piece work for me. It's just the prose parts that, I feel, are holding this piece back.

(Moving on!)

"Report," ordered Hughes. "Wait, belay that, there's a vehicle coming."

Outside, the Explorer rolled up the dirt road, as Staff Sergeant Arthur Chen, Corporal Munro and Specialist Onru beached the canoe.

This is not technically a run-on, but it's got way too many pauses. It should be snappier:

Outside, the Explorer rolled up the dirt road. Staff Sargeant Arthur Chen, Corporal Munro and Specialist Onru beached the canoe.

"Ma'am," Sergeant Ghazi said, as she readied her carbine. "My road guards just tried to send me something that the coghaz filters killed."

"Understood Sergeant. Order the rest of the watch to keep their distance and report to MTF command if they think we are compromised."

The SUV rolled to a stop in front of the cabin and the passengers got out.

This is a dramatic moment; you want to break this up a little into steps, giving it room to breathe — letting it escalate:

The SUV rolled to a stop in front of the cabin. The passengers got out.

The older woman looked up at Hughes who stood behind the partially open door, within the airlock like vestibule, with her sidearm ready and concealed. "Good morning, honey," the woman said, smiling broadly and squinting into the light, "Have you hea__". Then Hughes shot her.

This is a very dramatic, active moment that just goes off with a muffled squelch on account of how you're presenting it with prose.

The older woman looked up at Hughes. Tau-5's commander stood behind the partially opened door, her sidearm ready and concealed.

"Good morning, honey," the woman said. She smiled broadly and squinted into the light. "Have you hea—"

Hughes shot her.

With just a few paragraph breaks and some simple sentences, we create an enormous spike in dramatic tension. We go from a blocky paragraph filled with cumbersome compound sentences that just kind of sloshes its way over to a conclusion — to a series of brief, staccato statements separated by paragraph breaks, each of which ratchets the tension, the stakes — until we reach our finale ("Hughes shot her."). This is way more dramatic.

And the thing is, it's already here; I'm not adding anything to what you wrote — all I'm doing is reorganizing it a little. Shift a comma, split a compound into a simple sentence, add a few line-breaks — and something that's just kind of shuffling around becomes quick, fast, and tense.

In the membrane between the dimensions, where information interacts — as the Samsara troopers battled to retain their identity — the tendrils of soul-smoke were being ensnared by Cooper and Desai's outstretched threads. Within the saints' memeomes was information about their enemy and they launched their attack across the bridges formed where memes found their counterparts. Driven by their undying purpose, and armed with the Foundation's extensive documentation of this particular threat, the two saints began to methodically erase the alien information from existence.

Okay most of this next part is actually all pretty good and I have nothing to add or say about it.

Then the cloud shot tendrils out, racing with sudden speed towards the house.

Except that!


I think that's it. There's more I could talk about, but these are, like, the glaring things that are stopping me from upvoting. I'm not going to downvote, because — like I said — I really like this piece. I can't upvote because the prose is too soggy right now, though.

Anyway, I hope some of this helped (and I also hope it did not come off as hostile!). Good luck with this piece!

Only nitpick is that having the task force names show up in parentheses in the middle of dialogue felt awkward to read.

I am not sure what you mean. Do you mean in the manifestation log? I did it that way because I envisioned that Omega-Zero manifestations present as text files, and for the entities involved they are experienced more holistically as pure semiotics. Either way the standard format for MTFs seemed appropriate, since that information can obviously be conveyed in text.
